extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP lawyers, in-house counsel, judges, and advanced students interested in Korean patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing mediation, arbitration, civil remedies (injunctions, damages, employee invention compensation), appellate review, and criminal patent proceedings in the Republic of Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation initiation and referral
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation proceedings may be initiated by either party’s filing of a request for mediation with a court or by a court of the lawsuit’s referral to mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A case could start with mediation and return to litigation after mediation fails, or start in litigation, be referred to mediation, and then return to litigation if mediation fails. (Judicial Conciliation of Civil Disputes Act, arts 2, 6.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation venue and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation proceedings usually take place in a court’s mediation chamber on a scheduled date but may also be conducted in any other appropriate venue other than the courthouse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediation proceedings may be sealed from the public; however, a mediation judge may allow nonparties to attend the sealed proceedings where appropriate. (Judicial Conciliation of Civil Disputes Act, art. 9; art. 20.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of concluded mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation is duly reached by putting the matters agreed upon between the parties into the record; once mediation is reached at the mediation hearing, authentic copies of the mediation record are sent to the parties, and the mediation has the same effect as a judicial settlement in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Judicial Conciliation of Civil Disputes Act, arts 28–29.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory mediation ruling (ruling in lieu of mediation) and objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Where agreement has not been reached or where the terms are deemed inappropriate, a mediation judge or judge in charge may render a ruling to ensure a fair resolution (a 'ruling in lieu of mediation' or 'mandatory mediation ruling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mandatory mediation ruling has the same effect as a judicial settlement if neither party files an objection against the decision within two weeks from the date on which they received an authentic copy of the decision. (Judicial Conciliation of Civil Disputes Act, arts 30, 34(4).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of mediation and effect on litigation filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation proceedings are closed when mediation is not constituted or when an objection is filed against a mandatory mediation ruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lawsuit was filed before mediation, the case is shifted back to litigation; if mediation was sought without filing a lawsuit, a lawsuit is regarded to have been filed at the time the request for mediation was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Court mediation organization and use of mediation judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court established an internal mediation council of legal professionals and technical experts and has operated a mediation judge system to manage mediation cases and facilitate early mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Court may also entrust external institutions (e.g., Korean Commercial Arbitration Board) with mediation through memorandums of understanding. The use of mediation judges has increased applications and success rates (e.g., 45.8% successful mediation in 2019 across IP cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration definition and distinction from settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitration is a procedure to settle a dispute by an award of an arbitrator rather than by a court judgment and is fundamentally different from settlement and mediation which are agreements between the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitration is not disclosed to the public in principle, allows more flexibility in procedural formalities, and usually relies on a single-instance resolution (Arbitration Act, art. 3(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court dismissal when arbitration agreement exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should dismiss an action brought on a matter that is the subject of an arbitration agreement when the defendant raises the existence of an arbitration agreement as a defense, provided that the court does not find the arbitration agreement null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Arbitration Act, art. 9(1).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of arbitration agreements and optional clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: An arbitration agreement takes effect when the parties agree in writing to settle by arbitration all or part of a dispute; the effectiveness of an arbitration clause is determined by overall consideration of the meaning of arbitration, the nature and form of the agreement, and specific circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional arbitration clauses take effect when either party opts for arbitration and the other participates without objection; optional clauses only become effective upon such election and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of goodwill and reputation claim specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: When demanding restorative measures such as advertisements to reinstate goodwill or reputation in lieu of or in addition to damages, the plaintiff should specify in the complaint the specifics of such advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics include contents, size, font size and so on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee invention: definition and employer's automatic license
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee invention is an invention made by an employee in connection with their duties that falls within the scope of the employer’s business or present/past duties; an employer is automatically entitled to a free nonexclusive license to an employee’s invention (Invention Promotion Act, Article 10(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the employer succeeds the rights under contract or regulations, the employee is entitled to fair compensation (Invention Promotion Act, Article 15(1)). Provisions are intended to protect employees and are governed by civil law, labor law and patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements plaintiff must prove for employee invention compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim compensation the plaintiff should contend and prove: (i) that they invented the employee invention; (ii) that the defendant (employer) succeeded from the plaintiff the patent/utility model/design right (or rights to acquire them); (iii) that the employer earned sole and exclusive profits generated by the employee invention; and (iv) the scope of compensation for the employee invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical defenses include statute of limitations (10 years) or prior payments to the employee to be deducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship/contribution criteria for employee inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that the plaintiff is an inventor, it must be shown they are an employee, the invention falls within the scope of the employer’s business and duties, and the plaintiff contributed to the completion of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contribution examples: suggesting, adding or supplementing a concrete idea to solve technical problems; embodying a new idea through experiments; providing a specific means/method to achieve the purpose and effects; providing detailed advice or guidance enabling creation (Sup. Ct decisions cited). An employee can be a co-inventor only if they had a mutually cooperative relationship leading to completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer's 'profits' for compensation calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the employer is entitled to a free nonexclusive license even if they do not succeed the right, 'employer’s profits' when calculating compensation refers to the profits the employer is expected to earn by acquiring a sole and exclusive position to practice the employee invention that surpasses a nonexclusive license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced to Sup. Ct decisions interpreting Article 10(1) and compensation calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee invention compensation calculation factors and formula (A×B×C×D)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Invention Promotion Act sets forth following factors for calculation: (A) the profits the employer anticipates obtaining with the employee invention; (B) the employee’s ratio of contribution with respect to the employer’s contribution; (C) if joint invention, the employee’s ratio of contribution with respect to co-inventors; (D) if invention is a part/component of a multicomponent final product, the employee’s ratio of contribution to the final product. The formula is A × B × C × D (Article 15(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A is calculated by product sales revenue × hypothetical royalty rate × contribution ratio of the exclusivity of the right; B is (1 – employer’s contribution ratio). Use sales revenue of the final product for (A) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required for a permanent injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five elements to a permanent injunction: (1) the person seeking an injunction (patentee) — must be registered as patentee when argument at fact-finding trial is closed; (2) the party subject to injunction (infringer); (3) practicing the patented invention for business purposes; (4) specification of the infringing act and the defendant’s duty to disclose the specific act; and (5) infringement or likelihood of infringement (current or likely future acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nonexclusive licensee is not entitled to file for an injunction. Implementation for nonprofit business operations is still 'business purposes.' Plaintiff should specify each infringing act; if defendant fails to present specific conduct without justifiable reason, court may deem plaintiff’s allegations true. (Patent Act and cited Sup. Ct authority.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of permanent injunctions and related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope considerations include: what extent injunction covers whole product when patented invention is a part/component; claim for disposal of infringing products; and 'other measures necessary to prevent infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim for disposal must accompany a claim for injunction and specify products in an appendix. Courts have differed on whether injunction covers whole product or only infringing part; 'other measures' require balancing disadvantage to defendant versus disadvantage to patentee to avoid excessive burden. (Patent Act, art.126 and case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages: substantive elements plaintiff must prove
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain compensatory damages under the Patent Act and tort principles, plaintiff must prove: (i) the plaintiff is the patentee; (ii) the infringer has willfully or negligently infringed the patent/exclusive license; (iii) the infringement is unlawful; (iv) the infringer was capable of assuming liability at the time of infringement; (v) the patentee suffered damages; and (vi) proximate causation between infringement and damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Act presumes negligence by the infringer (Article 130). (Civil Act tort principles and Patent Act, art.128.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimant standing and apportionment for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimant seeking damages must be the patentee or exclusive licensee; a nonexclusive licensee does not have standing. For jointly owned patents, damages are typically awarded in proportion to each right holder’s percentage of ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sole nonexclusive licensee may pursue a tort claim in limited circumstances (infringement of credit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for calculating damages (four methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act recognizes four grounds in assessing damages: (i) loss suffered by the patentee (lost profits); (ii) the profits earned by the infringer (presumed to equal patentee’s loss); (iii) reasonable royalty (at minimum); and (iv) damages determined at the court’s discretion based on evidence and overall arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary damages may be awarded when it is difficult to produce evidence proving actual damages; the patentee may choose the most appropriate ground to plead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for damages claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for damages must be filed within three years from the date the plaintiff became aware of the damages caused by the infringement or within 10 years from the date of the infringement, whichever is earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action for damages based on an infringer’s unjust enrichment may be filed within 10 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits calculation and treatment of units exceeding patentee capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits are awarded for units the patentee would have sold but for the infringement, calculated by number of units × profit per unit, excluding units the patentee could not have sold for other reasons or units outside patentee production capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment effective Dec 10, 2020 allows patentee to recover reasonable royalty for infringing units transferred that exceed patentee’s production capacity (Article 128(2)(ii)). If transferred amount exceeds patentee capacity, amount equivalent to royalty in Article 128(5) can be awarded for excess units (with exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringer’s profits as basis for damages and profit theories
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, an infringer’s profit is often presumed to be the patentee’s lost profit; 'profit' includes all types of profits earned by the infringer through infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts commonly apply net profit theory (profit = sales revenue – [fixed costs + variable costs]) or marginal profit theory (profit = sales revenue – variable costs). Proving profits can be difficult, prompting courts to award discretionary damages when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine a reasonable royalty, courts may consider: the objective technical value of the patented invention; license agreements with third parties; license agreements with the defendant in the past; royalties for similar inventions in same technical field; remaining term of the patent; type of patentee’s use of the patent; existence of substitute technologies; and the infringer’s profits from the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee need not prove specific occurrences of loss to recover reasonable royalties. The reasonable royalty provision does not set a ceiling; patentee may also seek compensatory damages for amounts exceeding reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced damages for lack of willfulness or gross negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 128(6) allows the court to consider lack of willfulness or lack of gross negligence by the infringer when awarding damages, permitting a reduction in damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The infringer bears the burden to contend and prove lack of willfulness/gross negligence; reduced damages may not be lower than a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court’s discretionary damages determination
rubrics_metrics.description: When facts make it extremely difficult to prove the underlying facts for establishing amount of damages under other grounds, the Patent Act allows the court to determine a reasonable amount of damages by taking into account the overall purport of arguments and other relevant circumstances based on the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary awards are not arbitrary; courts typically state the calculation basis even when amount is determined at discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced (treble) damages and willfulness factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment effective July 9, 2019 provides for enhanced damages up to three times actual damages when infringement was willful; 'willful' means infringer acted while aware that the act would result in patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining willfulness, courts should consider: (i) whether infringer is in superior position to patentee; (ii) willfulness/awareness of likelihood of harm; (iii) significance of harm to patentee; (iv) economic benefits to infringer; (v) frequency and length of infringing act; (vi) criminal penalty for the act; (vii) financial status of infringer; and (viii) level of effort infringer exerted to provide relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review: de novo standard and evidence admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate proceedings are conducted on a substantially de novo basis; appellate court generally relies heavily on lower-court record but typically admits new evidence and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party requesting new evidence must explain failure to submit it in lower court; court will admit evidence considering circumstances such as expected harm to other party or need for expedited proceeding. Appellate hearings often close after first issue-by-issue review unless new evidence is introduced; parties hold technology review sessions followed by oral arguments (~20 minutes each) and judicial panel questions by issue. Parallel hearings may be held for concurrent infringement and IPTAB revocation cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate and Supreme Court timeframes and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts generally try to render decision within six months to one year from filing the appeal (longer for complex cases). The Supreme Court hears appeals on legal issues of material importance and typically renders decisions within one to two years if accepted for substantive review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court usually dismisses appeals summarily (without merits review) if they do not raise significant legal issues, typically within four months of record transfer. Appeals to Supreme Court usually handled by a panel of four justices; en banc review possible for major precedent issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal patent offenses and prosecutability change
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XII of the Patent Act provides criminal punishment for certain acts related to patent rights (e.g., patent infringement, divulgence of confidential information, perjury, false indication, fraud, breach of confidentiality orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment to Article 225(2) on Oct 20, 2020 changed patent infringement from an offense prosecutable only upon complaint to an offense prosecutable without the victim’s express complaint (i.e., prosecutable against the victim’s will).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for criminal patent cases (territorial and subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial jurisdiction for criminal patent cases follows ordinary criminal rules: court having jurisdiction over place of offense, defendant’s domicile/residence, or current location. Subject-matter jurisdiction: criminal patent cases are handled by a single-judge bench (unlike certain civil matters that may be panel cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patent crimes do not carry punishments triggering panel requirement under Article 32(1) of the Court Organization Act, all criminal patent cases are handled by a single judge.
